segments.text: When AI processes text, it first converts it into tokens
and gives each one a unique numerical token ID.
But by themselves, those numbers say absolutely nothing
about what the text actually means.
An ID identifies you.
It doesn't describe you.
Looking at these numbered badges,
the IDs tell you which student is which,
but they give zero information about who they really are,
whether they're funny, into hockey,
or the person who steals your French fries.
So to actually process language,
an AI needs a system that goes beyond
simple identification labels.
It needs a way to capture deep descriptive characteristics.
This table shows a thought experiment.
Imagine rating drinks on six specific characteristics,
sweet, bitter, fizz, heat, caffeine, and dark.
Each score runs on a scale from zero to 10,
where a higher number means more of that trait.
You and your friends tasted coffee
and rated it on six characteristics.
Let's put those readings in the table.
Coffee score is one for sweet, nine for bitter,
zero for fizz, nine for heat, eight for caffeine,
and 10 for dark.
Next, we add Coke.
It scores nine for sweet, one for bitter,
10 for fizz, two for heat, three for caffeine,
and eight for dark.
Compare them.
The one scoring nine sweet, one bitter,
and 10 fizz is Coke.
This row is a vector.
Each position is a dimension,
and its number is the value.
By combining these multiple distinct data points
into a single row,
we construct a unique mathematical fingerprint
for any item.
Now let's add Pepsi to the taste test.
Looking at its row,
you'll see that all six of its values match Coke exactly.
If you were to hide the drink names,
you would not be able to tell Coke and Pepsi apart
using only these six numbers.
Citrus gives us a seventh dimension.
We can now rate each drink for its citrus flavor
on that exact same zero to 10 scale.
With the new category in place,
coffee score zero, Coke scores one, and Pepsi scores 10.
Because of this single new trait,
their seven number profiles are now distinctly different.
Another dimension can capture a difference
the earlier numbers missed.
This shows why capturing real world complexity
requires a high volume of dimensions.
AI also uses numerical profiles to represent meaning.
Just as each drink has its own set of scores,
each token in an AI has its own row of numbers.
That row is called an embedding.
This comparison chart shows how our taste test
maps directly to an AI structure.
In your taste test, the three drinks get a row.
In AI, every token in the model's vocabulary gets a row.
In the taste test, we had seven dimensions.
In AI, there were typically thousands.
While you chose human ratings from zero to 10,
the AI learns its values during training,
resulting in a complex mix of positive numbers,
negative numbers, and decimals.
And where we provided clear labels like sweet and fizz,
AI dimensions have absolutely no labels.
They just capture abstract patterns
of how those tokens are used.
Both use a row of numbers to describe something.
This is the fundamental mechanism AI uses
to grasp context without human language.
Here is a diagram showing what happens inside a real model
when you type the word cat.
The system traces its token ID 4719,
directly to its matching row in the embedding table,
which sits right alongside other tokens
like dog, latte, and bicycle.
Looking across the top, we see the dimension columns,
D1 through DN.
Cat's row begins 0.45, then negative 0.23,
then 0.80, then 0.17, and continues across thousands
of positions to negative 0.35 in the last one.
A single learned number in this row is called a parameter,
and the entire row combined is the embedding.
It is worth noting that even pieces of words
receive their own embeddings.
If we split a word like unbelievable
into un, believe, and bull,
each of those pieces gets its own distinct row
of learned numbers.
AI uses numbers to work with meaning.
Those numbers help AI recognize similarities and differences.
